claims.claim: in microwave reheating the food's centre can stay cold while the outer parts and the container become hot
claims.definition: because microwave energy is absorbed within the first few centimetres and the field pattern is uneven, the interior heats by conduction and lags the outside
claims.measured_value: qualitative: centre temperature lags the shell by many tens of degrees in typical reheat loads; no single-number claim
claims.authoritative_source: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, 'Microwave Ovens and Food Safety'; Metaxas & Meredith, 'Industrial Microwave Heating' (1983)

nuance.note: directly follows from limited penetration depth + uneven field pattern; documented by USDA guidance on stirring/standing time

claims.claim: the popular claim that microwaves cook food from the inside out is false
claims.definition: the microwave field is absorbed in the outer layers; the interior is heated by conduction, the opposite of the folk picture
claims.measured_value: qualitative myth-correction; penetration depth of order centimetres (see f_penetration_depth)
claims.authoritative_source: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, 'Microwave Ovens and Food Safety' (addresses the inside-out myth explicitly)
claims.notes: the myth is the story's stated contradiction; the visual reveal localizes it at B3

nuance.note: myth-busting claim with an authoritative source; the correct mechanism is stated in positive form at B3/B7

claims.claim: microwaves penetrate only a few centimetres into wet food, so the outer shell absorbs the energy directly
claims.definition: the field amplitude decays exponentially with depth (skin/penetration depth); in water-rich foods at 2.45 GHz the penetration depth is of order 1-3 centimetres depending on composition, temperature and salt content
claims.measured_value: penetration depth of order 1-3 cm in typical moist foods at 2.45 GHz (composition-dependent); narration says 'only a few centimetres'
claims.authoritative_source: Metaxas & Meredith, 'Industrial Microwave Heating' (Peter Peregrinus, 1983); Datta & Anantheswaran, 'Handbook of Microwave Technology for Food Applications' (2001)
claims.notes: deliberately ranged: exact depth varies with salt/sugar/water content and temperature

nuance.note: exponential decay of microwave fields in lossy media is standard electromagnetics; the centimetre scale in food is textbook

claims.claim: a microwave oven heats food by dielectric heating: an oscillating electric field torques polar molecules (chiefly water) and molecular collisions dissipate the energy as heat
claims.definition: dielectric (dipole-rotation and ionic-conduction) loss converts electromagnetic field energy into thermal energy inside the material; the field alternates at the oven's 2.45 GHz carrier and polar molecules lag the swing, transferring energy in collisions
claims.measured_value: carrier frequency 2.45 GHz (wavelength about 12.2 cm in air); power of a typical domestic oven 700-1200 W
claims.authoritative_source: Metaxas & Meredith, 'Industrial Microwave Heating' (1983); IEEE definition of dielectric heating; US FCC Part 18 ISM allocations
claims.notes: established physics; narration phrases it as torqued dipoles and 'jostling neighbours' (dipole rotation + ionic conduction)

nuance.note: dielectric heating mechanism is standard physics; both dipole rotation and ionic conduction contribute, with the split depending on the food

claims.claim: 2.45 GHz is an international industrial-scientific-medical (ISM) band allocation chosen for regulatory convenience, not a special resonance frequency of water
claims.definition: liquid water's dielectric loss rises gradually over a broad band and its bulk absorption peak lies far above the oven band (tens of GHz at room temperature); ovens sit at 2.45 GHz because that band is reserved worldwide for ISM equipment
claims.measured_value: ISM band 2400-2500 MHz (centre 2.45 GHz); water's dielectric loss peak (room temperature, bulk liquid) lies in the tens of GHz range
claims.authoritative_source: ITU Radio Regulations ISM band allocations (Article 5.150); FCC Part 18; 'Dielectric heating' peer-reviewed treatments of water relaxation spectra (e.g., Kaatze, 'Microwave dielectric properties of liquids', Radiation Physics and Chemistry, 1995)
claims.notes: deliberate myth-correction of the '2.45 GHz = water resonance' legend; narration at B6 keeps the frequency point brief so the contested hot-spot claim carries the hedge

nuance.note: the ISM allocation history and the broadband (non-resonant) nature of liquid water absorption at 2.45 GHz are both documented; absorption depends on temperature and state, so no single resonance value is claimed

claims.claim: ice absorbs microwave energy far more weakly than liquid water because its molecules are bound in a rigid lattice, which is why defrost cycles use low power with rests
claims.definition: rotational relaxation of water molecules is mobility-dependent: in ice the dipoles are lattice-bound and the dielectric loss factor at 2.45 GHz is far below that of liquid water, so frozen food couples weakly to the field until it thaws
claims.measured_value: dielectric loss factor of ice at 2.45 GHz is orders of magnitude below liquid water near 0 degrees Celsius (temperature-dependent); defrost cycles typically duty-cycle a fraction of full power
claims.authoritative_source: Mudgett, 'Electrical properties of foods' in 'Microwaves in the Food Processing Industry' (1985); Metaxas & Meredith (1983); Kaatze, dielectric relaxation spectra of water and ice
claims.notes: narration stays qualitative ('barely answers the field'); defrost duty-cycle design follows

nuance.note: the ice/water loss contrast is textbook dielectrics; exact loss values depend on temperature and impurity content, so narration avoids numbers

claims.claim: the oven's energy pattern shifts with every food load and tends to concentrate energy in hot spots near edges, which turntables and stirrers average out
claims.definition: the field inside a loaded oven cavity forms a complex pattern from interference between the magnetron output, cavity geometry and the load itself; energy density is higher at some locations (commonly edges/corners), so rotating or stirring redistributes the load through the pattern
claims.measured_value: qualitative pattern claim; measured hot-spot maps vary strongly with cavity, container and food geometry
claims.authoritative_source: Metaxas & Meredith, 'Industrial Microwave Heating' (1983); Datta & Anantheswaran, 'Handbook of Microwave Technology for Food Applications' (2001); USDA guidance on stirring/rotating during microwaving
claims.notes: narration deliberately hedges: 'part standing wave, part food shape' — the exact pattern is geometry- and load-dependent, so no single causal picture is asserted

nuance.note: hot spots are real and documented, but their precise origin in a loaded cavity is model- and geometry-dependent (standing-wave structure, edge intensification, load shape all contribute); narration asserts only the hedged composite
